turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on through. We'll do a peak flow before the doctor sees you. Have you blown into one of these before?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, years back. I'm grand, it's only a small bit of a wheeze.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Seal your lips around it and blow out as hard and fast as you can. Grand. That one was 310.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure I wasn't ready. Doesn't mean much.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Once more, a big breath. 340. And a third one, 330. Best of the three is 340 litres a minute.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I think it was up around 500 the last time, or maybe that was years ago, I haven't a clue.

[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): I'll record 340 as today's best. Oxygen saturation is 96 percent, pulse 96 beats a minute, respirations 20 a minute, temperature 36.8. Take a seat, the doctor won't be long.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): How are you. I'm Dr. Brennan. The nurse has your peak flow at 340. What's been going on?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah it's nothing. I'm after having a cold and there's a bit of a wheeze hanging on. I'd have left it, only the cough was annoying the lads at work.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did the cold come on?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Eh, maybe ten days ago. Sore throat, runny nose, the usual. That's gone now, I'm grand on that front.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the wheeze itself, when did that start?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): A couple of days into the cold, so about a week. Only if I'm legging it up the stairs. Not when I'm sitting here. I'm not gasping or anything.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any cough with it?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): A small cough, yeah, mostly in the mornings. Nothing mad.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bringing up any phlegm?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Clear stuff. Not green. I already told them it wasn't a chest infection.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the chest? Any fever?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I felt a bit hot the first couple of days of the cold, but that's gone. No fever now.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you waking at night short of breath?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I sleep fine. I woke the once, but that was the dog barking, not the chest.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Your notes say asthma. Are you still using inhalers?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the puffers. The blue one and the brown one. I get them mixed up, to be honest with you.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): How have you been using them this week?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The blue one when I'm wheezy. Maybe five, six times a day the last few days. Two puffs a go.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the brown one?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): That's meant to be the everyday one, is it? I stopped that in March. Wasn't doing a thing, and I kept forgetting it.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you remember the name on the box, and the strength?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Beclomethasone, I think. The 200 one. They told me two puffs morning and night, but I haven't touched it since March.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. The blue one is salbutamol, 100 micrograms, two puffs, and you've been taking it five or six times a day. That's your reliever, not the preventer.

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): See, I had it backwards in my head. I thought the brown was for when you're bad and the blue was the daily one, or maybe the other way around. I never keep them straight.

[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): It's a common mix-up. Blue, salbutamol, is for the wheeze when it hits. Brown, beclometasone, you take every day, even on days you feel grand. You've been off the preventer since March, so the reliever is doing all the work.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I was flying all summer, so I didn't see the point. Sure I was grand.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Was there a tablet as well, montelukast?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Someone mentioned that. I never took it. Never even got a box.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): So no montelukast. Have you tried anything else for this spell?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): My flatmate had amoxicillin left in the press. I didn't take any of his. They're not my tablets.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Don't be taking anyone else's antibiotics, even if the box is sitting there.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah. It's not like I'm dying or anything.

[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me think this through out loud. A wheeze after a cold can be irritable airways, just post-viral, or it might be an asthma flare with the peak flow at 340 and you off the preventer. I am not calling this a chest infection, and I am not saying pneumonia. I won't settle it until I've listened to your chest.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Fire ahead. I'm telling you, it's mild.

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Breathe through your mouth for me, in and out. There's a wheeze on both sides, louder breathing out, and no crackles. Your throat is still a small bit red. You're talking in full sentences, no distress.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): See? I'm grand.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working impression is an acute flare of your asthma on the back of that viral cold, not an infection. That's provisional, and we'll judge it by how you get on with treatment.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So it's tablets, is it? I had prednisolone years ago, only took the one, and I was wired the whole night. I stopped it after that single tablet.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): A single tablet years ago isn't a course, and morning dosing should spare your sleep. I'm prescribing prednisolone 40 milligrams by mouth, once a day for five days, taken with food.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Five days. If you say so. Seems an awful lot for a small wheeze.

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): And back on the brown inhaler from today, beclometasone 200 micrograms, two puffs twice a day, every single day, including when you feel fine. Keep the blue salbutamol at two puffs, only when you actually need it, not five times out of habit.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): So brown every day, blue only if I'm wheezy. I'll try. No promises if I'm rushing out the door in the morning.

[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the blue inhaler isn't helping, if you can't finish a sentence, or if your lips look dusky, don't sit on it, go to the emergency department or straight back here. Otherwise I want you back in a week for a repeat peak flow.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): A week? I've work on. I'll come if I'm not better, maybe.

[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): No, book it anyway, not only if you're worse. Reception will slot you in on the way out. Morning prednisolone with your breakfast, brown inhaler morning and night, blue one for breakthrough wheeze.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand so. I'll take the script.
[SEG0054] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put the peak flow of 340 into the note so it's there for the review. Mind yourself.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, cheers. It's not that bad.
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you in a week. If you need the blue one on the way home, two puffs is grand, and then leave the rest to the new plan.

omissions.text: Patient had stopped the beclometasone preventer in March; this stop date is not recorded on the beclometasone medication entry.
Montelukast was specifically asked about and denied: patient never took it and never even got a box.
Patient denied taking leftover amoxicillin from the flatmate; antibiotics were considered and specifically not taken.
Patient reported no shortness of breath while sitting and said he was 'not gasping or anything'; this rest/no-gasping detail is not fully captured beyond shortness of breath at rest.
Doctor observed the patient was talking in full sentences; this specific examination finding is not recorded.
Doctor stated the differential/uncertainty explicitly: post-viral irritable airways versus asthma flare, and said he was not calling it a chest infection or pneumonia before examination.
Follow-up instruction was stronger than a generic 1-week review: doctor told patient to book the appointment anyway, not only if worse, with reception on the way out.
Doctor added immediate-use advice that if needed on the way home, salbutamol should be 2 puffs, then follow the new plan.
There was mild disagreement/hesitancy about treatment and follow-up: patient felt the wheeze was mild and prednisolone seemed 'an awful lot,' and was reluctant about the 1-week review due to work.
